items.summary:
Anthropic, the frontier AI firm behind the Claude chatbot, is floating on the US stock market in what has become history's largest initial public offering. The company raised a record sum of $107.3bn according to Sky News calculations; this figure includes another $26bn raised through a private sale of shares to tech firms. In a sign of strong investor demand, Anthropic increased the price at which it was selling its shares to $83 per share, up from an earlier guide of $70-$78. CEO Dario Amodei and fellow co-founders are expected to ring the Nasdaq opening bell at 9.30am New York time (2.30pm UK), after which the company will debut under the symbol "ANT".

The float arrives against a backdrop of market volatility, as tech stocks have fallen in recent weeks and pulled the Nasdaq Composite down by over 10% from its record high at the start of October amid Nvidia-related concerns. Anthropic itself remains loss-making: it posted an operating loss of over $8bn in 2025, with expenses of nearly $13bn outpacing revenues of $4.6bn. Revenues have accelerated in 2026, though the company faces the challenge of sustaining this growth and converting it into profits.

Garry White, chief investment commentator at Raymond James, described the IPO as a litmus test for market sentiment toward AI investing. He noted that a strong post-listing rally would signal markets remain convinced AI leaders can eventually generate sufficient profits to justify current spending on talent, infrastructure and computing power, whereas a weak reception or sharp decline could suggest investors are becoming more selective about converting rapid revenue growth into sustainable earnings.

In its prospectus, Anthropic devoted 90 pages of its SEC filing—around a quarter—to outlining risks. It warned that models may behave in unintended, misaligned or autonomous ways and cautioned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if not developed with appropriate safeguards.

Regulatory filings reviewed by Bloomberg News showed the lab sold just over 3.6 million shares to retail investors in the UK and close to 9.7 million shares to those in the European Union, Norway and Switzerland. Kathleen Brooks of XTB argued that Anthropic's trillion-dollar-plus valuation is more typical of a mature company with strong fundamentals than one it actually is; while revenue growth has been strong only in the short term, the firm remains unprofitable.

The share sale is expected to turn more than 4,000 staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. Anthropic's seven co-founders are all becoming paper billionaires through the deal: they are selling 23,648,646 shares worth $1.96bn out of the 980,000,000 Class A common shares being sold in the IPO, raising roughly $280m each for Dario and Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah.

Pre-market trading showed strong enthusiasm. Derivatives from IG International pointed to a market value of $1.35 trillion in Hong Kong Thursday morning—implying more than 24% above the IPO price—with the company's fully diluted market value roughly $1.5tn. Perpetual futures on Hyperliquid traded at around $101, about a 20% premium.

Hargreaves Lansdown reported that 45,811 of its clients applied for Anthropic shares; the average application was worth £6,661 and customers aged between 45 and 54 were the biggest buyers. However, those clients had only been allocated 33.6% of what they hoped to purchase. Chris Beauchamp of IG reported that retail demand alone exceeded planned allocations by more than 60%, describing overall demand as solid from both retail and institutional investors.

Roger Lee of Cavendish noted the record IPO priced above the top of its range, valued Claude's creator at $1.5tn, was more than 7x oversubscribed, and saw shares up around 20% pre-market—helping Nasdaq futures trade almost 2% higher.

Separately, Nationwide Building Society said it had used AI "extensively" in onboarding customers amid a record first half of the year for current account openings. Pre-tax profits surged 38% over six months to September compared with the same period last year, boosted by lower costs and higher revenues including a 7% rise in net interest income. CEO Debbie Crosbie said more than 30% of accounts were still opened in person at its branches, which it has pledged to keep operating until at least 2030 despite job cuts following the Virgin Money takeover.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva told world leaders at the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen that AI was already boosting growth. She said this year marked the first with a material impact on global growth, providing a counterbalance to negative energy supply shocks from Middle East turbulence while also fuelling inflation by pushing up prices.

Georgieva noted rapid AI-led acceleration across about a dozen economies contributed to 3.1% global growth and 3.4% for APEC—better than feared but worse than needed—and warned leaders faced "a genuine urgency" to advance AI-related policies, including digital infrastructure, labour markets and risk mitigation around financial stability and cybersecurity.

The item also reported that Nationwide's CFO Muir Mathieson said cost reductions related predominantly to technology and third-party expenditure rather than job cuts, as the number of employees and people-related costs actually rose amid plans to hire 800 more staff for its own-branded business bank accounts launching next year. Georgieva added that countries risk losing out without digital infrastructure ready for AI and with measures to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.
items.title: Anthropic's record $107bn IPO floats on Nasdaq amid AI market uncertainty

The Gentlemen ransomware group has added NVIDIA to its dark web data leak site, though it has not yet provided proof of a breach. The operation lists a countdown ending on November 28 and threatens to release stolen data if demands are met. In response, NVIDIA told BleepingComputer that it found no indication its systems or networks were affected but is now investigating an incident that may have impacted one of its service providers. A spokesperson stated: "NVIDIA is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner." The Gentlemen emerged last year as a closed ransomware group before switching to a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, offering affiliates up to 90% of ransom proceeds compared with the typical 70%-80%. It operates as a double-extortion group, exfiltrating data from victims' networks before encrypting systems and threatening online leaks. Since its emergence, it has claimed more than 1,100 victims across manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, energy, education, financial services, and other sectors. NVIDIA separately confirmed two earlier breaches: in May this year, some Armenian users' information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and usernames was exposed after a regional GeForce NOW Alliance partner was hacked, though the breach did not affect NVIDIA's network or operated services; and in March 2022, an attack claimed by the Lapsus$ gang affected more than 71,000 employees. The article also includes promotional content for Adaptive Security email protection tools.

No visual: separate facts about distinct incidents with no comparison across names.
items.title: NVIDIA Investigating Gentlemen Ransomware Breach Claims

items.summary: A letter to a forum, signed by Tan Lee Noi, advocates for integrating empathy-based moral education and critical thinking into the primary school curriculum. The author argues that children are born with a natural capacity for empathy, which should be nurtured early as it is essential for social and emotional development. Teaching students to respect and care for vulnerable sentient beings—including their peers and animals—is presented as a way to build emotional intelligence and perspective-taking ability. Citing research, the letter claims these competencies reduce classroom aggression, bullying, and antisocial behaviour, producing a safer learning environment. The author further contends that empathy education is most effective when paired with critical thinking, which teaches students to question assumptions, recognise biases, and evaluate motivations in order to resist peer pressure and misinformation. Together, the two approaches are said to benefit the wider community by fostering kinder, more resilient, and socially responsible citizens.
items.title: Letter advocating empathy and critical thinking in primary education

items.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI launches globally on November 19, and estimates from Sensor Tower place roughly three-quarters of the 17 million units sold so far on PlayStation, outselling Xbox. Shares in Sony rose almost 3% in Tokyo against a flat benchmark index. Analysts expect this worldwide enthusiasm to fall short in Japan, where Nintendo dominates gaming devices with its Switch 2 and consumers favor anime-style titles over realistic Western games. Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda said the current Japanese trends do not suit such a game and that there is no need for it to sell strongly at home; he added that Sony's benefits from royalties will be enormous while showing little desire to aggressively push hardware sales. In early 2026, Sony scored global success with Spider-Man: Brand New Day but faced competition in Japan from Chiikawa The Movie: The Secret Of Mermaid Island. Sorataka Goto of Kantan Games noted that Japanese gamers may struggle with the game's satirical elements and Western references, though worldwide hype is spilling over into unprecedented marketing for a Western-made title, including a large poster featuring characters Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in Akihabara; he predicted GTA VI would not become a mega blockbuster but will do very well. Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July-September quarter, down from 4 million a year earlier, which analysts see as demand ahead of GTA VI. Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote that PlayStation profits are modelled materially higher in coming quarters on account of the launch, and the release bolsters Sony's slate after it delayed God Of War Laufey by three months to May 2027; Sony is also grappling with procurement challenges as memory chip costs have risen sharply due to the AI boom. Goto said a few friends bought GTA VI at midnight but he was not in a hurry, since it is only on PS5 and Xbox and multiplayer online is unavailable yet, though he would consider buying once it reaches PC; he separately praised Nintendo's Switch 2 remake of The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time, which has sold more than five million copies in the first four days after its November launch.
items.title: GTA VI's Japanese market prospects amid Sony windfall

items.summary: On Nov 19, the High Court approved a $391.9 million collective sale of the leasehold rear block of The Centrepoint at 176A Orchard Road in Singapore. This followed reports that the Strata Titles Board had issued a stop order in August after two objections to the sale. After the board's decision, the collective sale committee applied to the High Court for approval. Before the Nov 19 hearing, the objecting owners Tanxuan Investments and an individual named Chin Yun Hee withdrew their objections. Lawyers for Tanxuan declined to comment on the nature of those objections due to confidentiality obligations, while Frasers Property and marketing agent Savills Singapore did not specify them either when asked. Observers note that common objections involve disputes over proceeds apportionment or collective sale price, or unit holders believing the sale was not conducted in good faith. On Feb 26, Frasers Property through its subsidiary Frasers Property Cuppage won the $391.9 million tender for the leasehold rear block. Under the agreed apportionment method, retail unit owners stand to receive between $840,000 and $9.29 million each, while apartment owners are expected to get between $2.65 million and $7.11 million per unit, subject to final adjustments. The Centrepoint was completed in 1983 and comprises a freehold front plot and the leasehold rear plot containing 66 retail units and 66 residential apartments on about 44,700 sq ft of land zoned commercial with a gross plot ratio of 5.6 and maximum height up to 10 storeys. The site occupies prime Orchard Road space with a direct sheltered link to Somerset MRT station. Frasers Property already held more than 52% of the rear block units by strata area before this sale, owns about 96% of the freehold front plot units, and fully owns 51 Cuppage Road, a connected 10-storey office building. A spokesperson said the acquisition strengthens its Orchard Road position and supports the government's masterplan to transform the precinct into a premier lifestyle destination. Savills Singapore managing director Jeremy Lake described this as the firm's fifth Orchard Road collective sale in recent years, with combined transaction value totalling nearly $2.7 billion. Separately, on Aug 31 Frasers announced its acquisition of Cuppage Terrace, a cluster of 17 conservation shophouses next to The Centrepoint for an agreed property value of $175 million, covering about 34,678 sq ft of gross floor area excluding the outdoor refreshment area. Savills Singapore's Jeremy Lake noted this marks its fifth Orchard Road collective sale in recent years with combined transaction value totalling nearly $2.7 billion.
items.title: High Court approves $391.9m collective sale of The Centrepoint's leasehold rear block

items.summary: As Silicon Valley figures increasingly become subjects of Hollywood productions, Sam Altman, founder and CEO of OpenAI, is set to appear as himself in the biographical comedy-drama 'Artificial,' starring Andrew Garfield. The film chronicles OpenAI's rise alongside the internal turmoil that followed his brief ousting from the company in 2023, with a theatrical release scheduled for Christmas. Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Altman said he was no longer struck by the prospect of being portrayed in a movie, noting it would have seemed very strange to him two decades ago but is now among the least surprising things about his life. He identified what he considers genuinely weird: ushering in technology while carrying significant responsibility for its success amid real concerns. The article also contrasts Altman's reaction with Mark Zuckerberg's response to 'The Social Network,' which depicted Facebook's founding and, per Zuckerberg, mischaracterized his motivations despite accurate details like clothing. Zuckerberg reportedly organized a company outing when the film released and purchased an Ardsley High School T-shirt worn by co-star Jesse Eisenberg at auction, while Eisenberg has distanced himself from being associated with Zuckerberg. Regarding Garfield, who is known for Spider-Man and previously played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in 'The Social Network,' Altman had not yet been interviewed about the film as of publication.
items.title: Sam Altman Unfazed by Andrew Garfield Portrayal in 'Artificial'

items.summary: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it is enabling developers to build AR Lenses using their existing AI coding assistants, including Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses are augmented reality effects used across the platform to alter appearance, add digital objects, or create interactive camera experiences. The company introduced Easy Lens CLI as an extension of its earlier Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on web and mobile; the new command-line version brings that same approach into developers' existing workflows so AI assistants handle technical work while creators focus on vision. Snapchat frames the launch as a way to lower barriers for AR content creation and reach more developers who increasingly rely on AI coding tools, rather than requiring them to learn Snapchat's own development environment. Creators enrolled in Snapchat's Lens+ Payouts program can earn money from Lenses built with Easy Lens CLI; the company reported paying out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month. According to Snapchat, developers describe their desired Lens in plain language and the AI assistant manages the full process: building using more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, publishing to Snapchat, and tracking performance. The tool reportedly supports Web Lens games with leaderboards as well as camera effects and beauty filters, and can move a game from initial idea to published Lens within a single day without developers writing code themselves. Snapchat says the capability lets AI assistants generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to a creator's phone. The tool is aimed at multiple creator types: game developers who can bring existing browser games as Web Lenses, AI creators using assets from their preferred tools in their own style, and agencies or brands that can convert campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time. Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
items.title: Snapchat Adds AI Coding Assistants to Its Lens Creation Tooling

items.summary: A pattern has emerged across leading AI laboratories in which safety researchers and engineers are leaving their jobs to issue public warnings that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI's product releases quit because he described the company's culture as 'broken' and said the entire AI industry was too careless about developing the technology. The previous month, a researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, left warning that he believed AI 'could kill us all by the end of the decade'. Isabelle Ferreras argues these resignations reveal a deeper institutional failure: when exit becomes the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm, it signals broken corporate governance and takes with each departure the knowledge needed to steer systems safely. She notes that policymakers, tech workers, trade unionists, members of parliament, and experts from institutions including the Vatican and the UN are gathering in London this week to discuss AI safety, but contends regulation cannot be safe from outside if companies remain autocracies on the inside. Ferreras criticizes regulatory debates for treating AI either as a consumer product tested for defects or as a geopolitical race won by relaxing rules, citing Ursula von der Leyen's EU digital omnibus, which delays implementation of requirements in the 2024 AI Act covering 'high-risk' systems, at the encouragement of corporate lobbies arguing legislation imposes too many burdens. She stresses that AI is not merely software but a technology of government, and inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google, executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models shaping millions of lives. Referencing Jeremias Adams-Prassl's research on the gig economy and automated work in Europe, she notes algorithmic management already monitors, evaluates and dismisses workers without human oversight. Drawing on Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, Ferreras argues technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity because institutions decide who benefits and who pays; citing Hélène Landemore's concept of 'democratic reason', she frames extending democracy into the firm as a practical necessity for ethical judgment. She proposes three reforms: first, protecting AI developers by outlawing non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, enacting whistleblower protection, and giving tech workers collective standing over corporate strategy with independent reporting channels and formal representation before model deployment; second, establishing a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI after the Meta case where Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp introduced tools tracking employees' keystrokes, mouse clicks and screen content for training data, requiring prior negotiation of any monitoring system plus collective bargaining on AI deployment, veto rights for works councils or trade unions backed by independent technical experts, and a strict ban on automated firing; third, democratizing boardrooms through worker-elected directors moving toward dual-majority governance where strategic decisions require consent from both capital and labour. Ferreras warns that leaving governance to self-regulation and occasional whistleblowers will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy, arguing accountability begins with giving builders of these systems and those they govern an enforceable voice from the code floor to the boardroom.
items.title: AI safety whistleblowers resigning signals broken corporate governance

The official Amazon Black Friday sale launched on November 19, beginning at 12:01 a.m. PT / 3:01 a.m. ET with millions of price drops across electronics, home goods, apparel, gaming gear, and more. The event is framed as a 12-day run extending through Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, though the official Black Friday sale itself ends on Saturday, November 28 at 3:00 a.m. ET before transitioning into its weekend-long Cyber Monday promotion. Throughout the period Amazon offers daily themed deal drops of up to 60% off.

Apple deals include AirPods Pro 3 now $179 (regularly $249), an even lower price on AirPods Max 2 at $429 ($120 off, regularly $549), AirTag 2 packs matching all-time lows of $23 for a single unit and $70 for four units, the Apple Watch Series 12 lineup ranging from $329 to $479 with regular prices up to $60 higher, MacBook Neo starting at $650 (regularly $700), M5 MacBook Air models discounted by $200 or $250 depending on configuration, and the Apple Pencil (USB-C) at $69 (regularly $79). Amazon Devices offers include its all-new Android Alexa Tablets from $150 all-time lows, plus Fire TV Stick 4K down to $20 (regularly $60), a Fire TV Cube for $90 (regularly $200), and various other Fire TV models. Google deals feature up to $100 off the Pixel Watch 5 lineup with specific prices of $300, $330, $400, and $430 depending on size and connectivity, plus as much as $450 off the Pixel 11 series phones starting at $699 (regularly $899) for the base model. Samsung offers include up to $450 off its Z Fold 8 lineup with specific prices of $1,550 and $1,750 for the 256GB and 512GB models respectively against regular prices of $1,900 and $2,100, alongside S26 Ultra phones discounted from $950 to $1,150.

PlayStation deals include DualSense controllers from $55 (regularly $75+), a DualSense Edge controller for $170 (regularly $200), the PULSE Elite headset at $110 (regularly $150), and numerous game titles discounted by roughly half their regular prices. The article notes that many notable offers are not highlighted on Amazon's main sale page, directing readers to 9to5Toys.com for curated deals.

Regarding whether better deals will appear next week, the source states it is possible with additional products added each day through Thanksgiving and Black Friday, but asserts that big-ticket items tend to drop when the sale begins and see only minor price reductions as it progresses.
