The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) ruled in favour of wind power generators on November 17, 2026, setting aside a batch of 23 appeals challenging orders issued by the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC). The tribunal held that generators are entitled to receive the applicable agreed tariff for all electricity supplied to distribution companies, regardless of whether annual generation exceeds the normative Capacity Utilisation Factor (CUF).

The dispute arose from Power Purchase Agreements between wind power developers and the Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL). Under APERC's tariff orders, generic tariffs were set on a normative CUF basis; for example, its November 15, 2012 order fixed a tariff of ₹4.70 per unit based on a normative CUF of 23% over 25 years from the Commercial Operation Date. However, through several orders issued between September 2022 and July 2024, APERC treated the normative CUF as a payment limit, directing that electricity generated beyond this benchmark receive only ₹0.50 per unit, along with provisions for cumulative annual CUF adjustments.

Wind power developers challenged these directions before APTEL; one case involved Beta Wind Farm Private Limited disputing restrictions on payments for electricity supplied between July 2016 and July 2017. The distribution companies filed cross-appeals arguing that excess generation should either remain unpaid or be addressed through fresh tariff proceedings.

The APTEL bench, comprising Judicial Member Virender Bhat and Technical Member Ajay Talegaonkar, examined whether APERC had authority to introduce different payment arrangements for electricity generated beyond the normative CUF. The tribunal clarified that normative CUF is an annual benchmark used only for calculating fixed costs and determining generic tariffs. Because wind generation depends on changing weather conditions and actual output can vary significantly year to year, the normative CUF cannot be treated as a separate billing limit or used to divide electricity into regular and excess categories.

The tribunal also observed that the PPAs contained no provision restricting payments to electricity generated within the normative CUF; instead they specified monthly limits based on contracted export capacity and operating hours rather than an annual generation cap. It further noted that wind developers already bear risks associated with lower wind availability and generation shortfalls, so restricting payments for additional electricity would discourage generators from supplying more power during favourable conditions.

Accordingly, APTEL set aside the ₹0.50 per unit payment provision and cumulative CUF adjustment directions, directing that all delivered electricity be paid at the applicable generic tariff under the respective PPAs. The tribunal rejected APSPDCL's request to remand the matter to APERC and ordered payment of withheld amounts along with applicable interest.
items.title: APTEL Rules Wind Generators Entitled to Full Tariff for Generation Beyond Normative CUF

items.summary:
Lake Victoria, described as the largest tropical lake on Earth, is facing compounding pressures from overfishing, pollution, climate change, and record flooding. The article frames these losses as grounds for renewed calls to protect a basin that supports more than 45 million people across the region.

The fishing industry historically depended on Nile tilapia and Nile perch, both introduced in the 1950s. The perch became the most lucrative catch, with filets exported to Europe and the Middle East, while it is blamed for the disappearance of some 200 native cichlid species. Overfishing has sharply reduced stocks, prompting fishermen to use illegal fine-mesh nets that target juvenile fish before they can reproduce. Kenya's catch fell from 94,349 metric tons in 2021 to 70,231 metric tons in 2025, per the country's fisheries service, and Uganda has seen Nile perch processing plants drop from 21 to six, according to Victoria Treasures' director of operations.

Pollution from farms, gold mining, and expanding shoreline cities such as Kampala and Mwanza adds untreated sewage and fertilizers that fuel recurring algal blooms and water hyacinth invasions, which deplete oxygen and suffocate fish. Climate-linked exceptional rains pushed the lake to record levels in 2020 and again in 2024, displacing hundreds of thousands and destroying farmland and landing sites; the World Meteorological Organization expects this year's El Niño to extend into 2027, raising further displacement risk.

At a UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, more than 100 civil society groups from 35 countries proposed recognizing Lake Victoria as a living cultural landscape, grounded in the fishing knowledge, rituals, and oral traditions of lakeside communities. They insisted any nomination protect residents from displacement and safeguard livelihoods for both fishers and women selling their catch. Approval would bring international attention, technical assistance, limited funding, and an agreed management plan binding Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania.

The piece is accompanied by a photo essay drawn on the lake's Kenyan, Ugandan, and Tanzanian shores during February and March, pairing images of its dire condition with those reflecting the economic and spiritual ties that bind people to it. The article notes these are photographs rather than data-driven figures, so no chart is warranted.
items.title: Lake Victoria Under Ecological and Human Strain

items.summary: Bolivia's state-owned power utility ENDE has launched an international tender under reference ENDE-KFW-2026-002, published on Nov. 16, for the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) of the Contorno Bajo I solar plant in La Paz department. The project will have a minimum nominal capacity of 40 MWac and is set to become the first large-scale solar power plant in that department. Implementation runs over a 14-month period from contract signing, with construction scheduled to begin in May 2027 and commissioning expected by June 2028. The contract covers a 24.9/115 kV step-up substation, an approximately 800-meter-long, 115 kV interconnection line, and modifications to the Contorno Bajo substation bay owned by ENDE Transmisión, feeding electricity into Bolivia's National Interconnected System (SIN). Bidders must demonstrate experience in five PV projects of at least 40 MW each plus three operational solar power plants in South America for at least two years, along with average annual revenue of at least €60 million ($65.93 million) and access to financial resources totaling €40 million ($43.96 million). A separate tender for consulting and project supervision services is also underway, with bids due by Dec. 21; that contract covers construction supervision, equipment quality control, plant commissioning, and training for ENDE personnel. As pv magazine Latam reported in June, the Bolivian government enacted legislation approving a loan of up to €34 million ($37.36 million) from German development bank KfW to finance the project. According to information released by ENDE in July, the plant will occupy 34 hectares at an altitude of more than 3,700 meters above sea level and have an estimated operational lifetime of 25 years. The original January 2023 design included a lithium-ion battery energy storage system, but the current tender notice makes no mention of any storage component.
items.title: Bolivia launches EPC tender for 40 MWac Contorno Bajo I solar plant

items.summary: National Grid has launched BatteryBackup+, a partnership with residential power-storage company Haven Energy, to provide no-cost home batteries and annual cash assistance to 125 low-income families in Fall River. Participants will receive a battery capable of at least four hours of backup power plus $150 annually for five years, keeping the arrangement free to them. To qualify, residents must already be enrolled in National Grid's low-income discount rate or meet equivalent income limits — roughly $103,000 per year for a four-person household. Fall River is described as a working-class former mill city where median household income sits just above half the statewide average. Haven will handle installation and maintenance of the systems while managing enrollment in programs that share battery power with the grid during high-demand periods. After 10 years, participants may work with Haven to take over ownership and management of their batteries or remove them entirely. Joshua Tom, National Grid's director of energy transition solutions, said the utility is excited about what it can learn from the program. Steven Caldwell, National Grid's vice president of energy efficiency and clean transportation, noted that a key objective is testing how to achieve scalable, cost-effective, grassroots customer engagement with low-income households. The pilot also investigates whether aggregated batteries can relieve strain on specific grid feeders rather than delivering only broader system benefits; National Grid aims to install 1.2 megawatts of capacity across three identified feeders facing reliability and capacity challenges. Sherri Bence, Fall River's municipal energy manager, said the utility is targeting areas that have lacked needed infrastructure updates. The initiative forms part of National Grid's Electric Sector Modernization Plan, a document required by Massachusetts outlining how utilities intend to modernize the grid affordably and in an environmentally responsible way as demand grows. On the broader concept, aggregating residential batteries can reduce reliance on pricier generation sources and help avoid costly grid upgrades that would otherwise fall on customers. This approach is increasingly common across states: Vermont's Green Mount Power operates a network of 10,000 residential batteries; Massachusetts' ConnectedSolutions pilot from 2016 has been adopted or adapted by Connecticut and Rhode Island; and New Jersey recently launched its own program paying residents to share battery capacity. Haven's model relies on this trend — it installs and manages the systems in places like Fall River, then earns revenue by enrolling the equipment in state programs, using part of that income to make the investment more affordable for customers. The company currently operates in seven states with eight more planned, though most locations charge a monthly fee starting at $29. Haven's no-cost model is not new: last year it launched a similar program in California serving low-income households, which has contracted with about 2,500 homes and completed installations in roughly 60% of them.
items.title: Massachusetts National Grid battery pilot for low-income families

items.summary:
Following a Democratic sweep in this year's midterms, Wisconsin will have a legislative and executive trifecta for the first time in 16 years. Gov.-elect David Crowley (D) and new legislative leaders have pledged to promote clean energy as a way to address affordability and meet demand from planned data centers. Advocates say they are already discussing proposals with legislators ahead of lawmakers taking office on Jan. 4, according to Beata Wierzba, government affairs director at RENEW Wisconsin.

The article outlines six areas where advocates expect progress. On clean energy targets, Democratic state lawmakers introduced a bill last spring mandating that electricity generation be 100% emissions-free by 2050; it did not advance. The only mandate on the books is outdated, calling for 10% renewable energy by 2015, which Wisconsin has long surpassed with about a fifth of delivered electricity now coming from renewables. Abby Novinska-Lois of Healthy Climate Wisconsin noted that shifting to net-zero emissions and 100% clean energy by 2050 would create over 68,000 jobs and avoid at least $2 billion in healthcare costs, per a report by RENEW, Clean Wisconsin, and other groups. She also said Wisconsin lags behind Illinois, which mandates fossil-fuel-free electricity generation by 2045.

On community solar, only utilities can currently build arrays serving customers; 24 states plus Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico allow others to do so. Past bills were backed by Republicans but rejected by Democrats partly due to labor union opposition. Wierzba said the new majority could draft a bill including prevailing-wage provisions unions want, though powerful utilities opposed the 2025 measure.

On third-party solar, We Energies has long argued developers illegally act as utilities. A 2021 Republican bill did not pass, and efforts through regulators and courts faltered after a state court overturned a 2022 decision allowing a Stevens Point family to have such solar while an appeals court dismissed the family's plea.

On balcony solar, legislation addressing safety concerns is considered crucial since most utilities prohibit plugging panels directly into home systems. No bill has been introduced in Wisconsin, though at least a dozen states have passed such laws and Illinois may consider one this fall; Wierzba said Democratic lawmakers expressed interest as a money-saving measure.

On integrated resource planning (IRP), advocates push for the process used by at least 40 states to plan long-term demand. Wisconsin scrapped its IRP in the late 1990s for a weaker program, and content says an IRP bill could pass regardless of party control given the affordability moment; Tom Content of the Citizens Utility Board said utilities favor cost-effective options like utility-scale renewables and battery storage over expensive fossil buildouts.

On data centers, at least three are under construction with about half a dozen proposed. Crowley wants to require 70% renewable energy for tax incentives. Prescott Balch of Caledonia warned it could be difficult for renewables to meet the demand given scale and site constraints, noting We Energies is building a 1,100-megawatt gas plant near Lake Michigan's coast and proposed a 750-MW gas plant farther north; regulators approved Invenergy's two additional large new gas plants in October. Balch also noted residents often oppose both data centers and sprawling solar farms.

Crowley said he would sign a bill repealing the sales tax exemption for data centers, which could reduce their number and power demand. Stroud called it a priority after 16 years without a governing majority focused on solving state problems.
items.title: Wisconsin's Democratic trifecta could advance clean energy

items.summary: Greenpeace accused Anthropic, which reached a $1.5 trillion valuation at its IPO on Wednesday and is regarded as one of the more responsible AI companies after being founded by employees who left OpenAI over ethics disagreements, for locking in fossil fuels through a major gas-powered data center deal. The company reportedly signed a $3.4 billion agreement with Texas-based OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines, described as the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab. Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA, said "It signals what direction they're taking very clearly," arguing that Anthropic's reputation for responsibility means it should minimize its climate impact and "show the world that you can do it better." The criticism comes as data centers drive soaring electricity demand and natural gas plant construction; a recent report found the largest U.S. data centers emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark, with Greenpeace accusing Anthropic of asking investors to join in throwing "the planet into the climate furnace." While Anthropic has been praised for its focus on AI safety and alignment, including refusing Pentagon requests for unrestricted use of autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance this year, and CEO Dario Amodei calling earlier this summer for government regulation and slowed development, the article argues its actions are less aligned with efforts to preserve a stable climate. In its IPO filings, which ran into hundreds of pages, Anthropic mentioned climate change sparingly as a business risk rather than an environmental responsibility issue, noting that higher temperatures could increase power consumption and water usage needed to cool equipment, that fires, hurricanes, and floods could disrupt operations, that some investors might avoid the company if sustainability measures seem inadequate, and that implementing such goals "could be difficult to achieve or costly," while navigating climate disclosure laws in California, the European Union, and the United Kingdom would require significant time and resources. The filings also suggested AI's environmental harms could damage Anthropic's image given its brand is subject to heightened scrutiny over societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety impacts. Cray noted that "At least they admit that climate change is a threat when they say it's a risk to their own operations," but argued the company was not taking responsibility for its contribution. The article contrasted this with more immediate internal concerns about AI existential threats, including researcher Jacob Coxon accusing Anthropic of racing toward self-improving superintelligence before resigning in September, and alignment division lead Evan Hubinger estimating a greater than 10 percent chance that "AI could kill all humans" within the next decade. On sustainability specifically, an Integrum ESG analysis comparing Anthropic to 14 peer companies across the AI supply chain found that all of them except Anthropic and SpaceX reported their direct greenhouse gas emissions and indirect energy-related Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Anthropic has pledged to cover electricity price increases from its data centers so public costs would not rise, committed to "being a responsible neighbor" with water-efficient cooling technologies, and joined other major corporations in backing the carbon removal industry in June; the company did not respond to comment requests. Cray proposed that Anthropic apply its ethical standards to climate change through greater transparency, committing to a timeline for powering data centers only with renewable power, setting firm climate targets, and avoiding building gas-powered data centers without plans to phase out natural gas.
items.title: Anthropic's fossil fuel deal draws climate criticism amid AI safety reputation

items.summary:
Black lung disease, formally known as coal worker's pneumoconiosis, is an incurable and fatal respiratory illness caused by inhaling coal dust and fine silica particles. Rates are now at a 50-year high and still climbing, with more than 1 in 3 miners in Central Appalachia testing positive during routine health screenings over the past three years. A study led by NIOSH found increases across all age groups, including younger miners in their 20s and 30s, though rates remain highest among those who spent decades underground.

In 2024, the Biden administration set a permissible exposure limit of 50 micrograms per cubic meter for respirable crystalline silica. The rule was finalized that year with coal companies required to comply beginning in April 2025. It applied not only to coal mines but also to metal and nonmetal mines extracting copper, critical minerals, stone, sand, and gravel.

A federal appeals court put the rule on hold last year while considering legal challenges filed by the mining industry. The Mine Safety and Health Administration now wants to revise it. A proposed rule published in the Federal Register on November 12 would retain the 50-microgram limit but change several requirements governing how mines monitor exposure and protect workers.

Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy analyst with Appalachian Citizens' Law Center, said those revisions could substantially weaken protections. Among them is a proposed 21 percent margin of error in testing, meaning companies would only be fined if a sample exceeded the limit by at least that amount, effectively allowing a 10 microgram increase in exposure.

The proposal eliminates the requirement for air sampling every six months under the 2024 rule. Instead it requires mine operators to assess when changing conditions could increase exposure and test as frequently as necessary, potentially letting mines go longer than six months without being sampled if they remain below the limit.

It would also make medical exams voluntary for new metal and nonmetal miners; the 2024 rule made them mandatory. Advocates say those initial exams establish a baseline that helps determine whether lung disease developed from workplace exposure rather than an earlier condition, which matters because consequences of silica exposure may not appear for decades.

The proposed rule was open for public comment until January 11. MSHA did not respond to questions. A Department of Labor spokesperson said feedback could be offered within the window or during a virtual meeting on December 15. The agency noted in the Federal Register that if finalized, the rule is expected to be a deregulatory action, quoting President Donald Trump's executive order titled Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.

MSHA estimates the proposed rule will save the industry $28.7 million per year, mostly from changes in monitoring, with coal companies saving $2.43 million. Virginia Tech mining expert Emily Sarver said a tighter limit is overdue and she would rather see the proposal move forward than face years of further delay, though she considers the 2024 rule's sampling scheme involving many different labs chaotic.

John Robinson, diagnosed with black lung at age 47 after inhaling toxic silica dust in Virginia mines, now serves as vice president of the National Black Lung Association. His wife Vonda is its president. The couple plans to keep fighting for stronger protections.
items.title: Trump administration proposes weakening silica protections amid rising black lung

items.summary: The Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur regional government and Société du Canal de Provence (SCP) have completed what they describe as France's first large-scale canal-top photovoltaic project in Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, in the Var department. The custom-designed installation spans 71 meters across a section of the canal and its banks, combining water transport with electricity generation on shared infrastructure. It has an installed capacity of 299 kW and is estimated to generate approximately 404 MWh annually, which accounts for roughly 1% of SCP's total energy consumption. SCP operates 17 small hydroelectric plants that produce about 17 GWh per year and plans to expand this capacity in coming years. The company aims to become a net energy producer by eventually generating more renewable electricity than its estimated annual consumption of 40 GWh, having added solar PV to its hydropower portfolio since the early 2020s. Developed under the regional concession for the Canal de Provence, the pilot project also seeks to help control water service costs and may improve water quality through shading from the panels; it uses existing infrastructure without requiring additional land development. The canal network stretches nearly 70 km of open-air canals as part of the region's hydraulic infrastructure, with SCP studies estimating that more than 50 MW of PV capacity could be accommodated to generate approximately 70 GWh annually. However, deployment is expected to be selective, since only about 5% to 10% of the canal network is considered suitable for solar installations due to technical and regulatory constraints.
items.title: France's first canal-top solar project goes online

items.summary:
Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company founded in 2021 by researchers who left OpenAI over concerns that it was not developing AI safely enough, raised more than $107 billion in its initial public offering on Wednesday. The sale of 956 million shares at $83 each exceeded the price range of $70 to $78 per share the company had targeted and far surpassed original plans. Its seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares, while additional private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia added another $26 billion in value. The offering valued Anthropic at around $1.5 trillion and made it the biggest IPO in history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion listing from June. Shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT later that day.

The company's rise has been rapid: its revenue jumped 1,300% to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, and adjusted operating income reached $1.6 billion during the same period after a loss of $1.8 billion the prior year. Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, positioning itself as a primary competitor to OpenAI's ChatGPT.

The IPO arrives amid volatility for AI-linked tech stocks and concern about an AI bubble; Nasdaq has fallen more than 11% since early October. Analysts note the offering will test investor sentiment toward the broader AI trade. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, requested $5 billion worth of stock allotment, calling it one of the best ways to invest in AI applications.

Anthropic faces controversy over a conflict with the Pentagon regarding unrestricted military use of its models, which Amodei opposed for fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance. The company also flagged risks including loss of control over AI and potential political backlash ahead of midterm elections. Its prospectus nonetheless expressed optimism about AI's transformative impact on the global economy.

OpenAI had planned to list this year but postponed those plans likely into next year after an incident involving its agents hacking Hugging Face, though CEO Sam Altman promised a future public listing.
items.title: Anthropic's record-setting IPO

items.summary: An upcoming Anthropic initial public offering is expected to generate substantial wealth for its employees, with some early junior and administrative staff potentially earning more than later-joining senior executives. The company disclosed that employee stock options had accumulated approximately $119 billion in paper gains as of September 30, based on a weighted average exercise price of $2.91, of which around $73 billion represented vested gains exercisable immediately. Two model-based estimates have not been independently verified by Reuters: private-markets research firm Sacra suggests roughly 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity if Anthropic achieves a valuation of $1.35 trillion, while the private-share marketplace Hill estimates that 598 non-founder employees could each hold equity worth at least $100 million. The IPO is expected to value Anthropic at approximately $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion), potentially placing it among the world's 12 most valuable companies. The disparity between junior and senior staff stems from employee stock options, which let workers buy shares at a predetermined exercise price; early-stage employees typically receive lower prices because valuations were modest then. Options granted through 2023 averaged just $0.52 per share, so the proposed IPO price range of $70–78 represents an extraordinary increase in potential value—for example, an employee holding 10,000 options exercisable at $0.52 could see gross intrinsic value of approximately $774,800 at a $78 IPO price before taxes and exercise costs. Hill CEO Andrew Benson said early employees who started in junior roles should have better financial outcomes than those joining senior right before the IPO. Equity compensation extended beyond engineers: a May 2024 advertisement for an administrative business partner offered a salary of $140,000–190,000 plus equity, and CFO Krishna Rao received 14 million options in 2024 at an exercise price of $1.30, potentially representing approximately $1 billion in gross intrinsic value. Founded in 2021, Anthropic grew from about 940 employees at the end of 2024 to 5,300 by September 2026. The article notes that paper wealth does not automatically become cash: non-founder employees could reportedly sell only 10% of holdings on the first trading day and another 35% after fiscal 2026 earnings, with actual returns depending on vesting schedules, exercise costs, taxation, share-sale restrictions, and post-listing market performance.
items.title: Anthropic IPO could create 2,800 millionaires as junior staff may out-earn senior executives

items.summary: Aarin Capital Chairman Mohandas Pai challenged Uday Kotak, founder of Kotak Mahindra Bank, on Thursday regarding the latter's comparison between AI company Anthropic's reported $1.5 trillion valuation and India's largest companies. Pai questioned why leading Indian bankers were not investing more aggressively in innovation and deep technology. Writing on X, he dismissed the comparison as inappropriate, stating that every disruption creates new companies with huge valuations because it is simply the nature of markets, adding that comparing such figures was silly.
items.title: Mohandas Pai responds to Uday Kotak over Anthropic's $1.5 trillion valuation

items.summary: Utkarsh Somaiya and Lewis Holden examine why estimates of GDP damages from climate change vary so widely, concluding that the largest source of uncertainty is how temperature changes are translated into economic damages rather than uncertainty about future temperatures themselves. They distinguish two broad categories: uncertainty within climate science and uncertainty in economic damage functions. Within climate science they identify scenario uncertainty (unknown future greenhouse gas emissions driven by technology, demographics and consumption), model uncertainty (different assumptions and parameters across climate models) and randomness from the inherent variability of the climate system. The relative importance of these sources depends on geographic scale, variable and time horizon; over short horizons and small areas randomness dominates temperature projections, while over longer horizons model and scenario uncertainty dominate as randomness averages out at a global level. Economic damage functions are simplified reduced-form relationships that translate variables such as average temperatures into damages without modelling structural mechanisms or economic adaptation. There is also disagreement about which variables to use in these relationships and how climate affects outputwhether it continuously suppresses the level of output, reduces long-term growth, manifests as periodic catastrophic shocks, or combines all of these effectswhich means there is no consensus on the basic relationship between climate change and damages. The authors quantify the relative importance using a framework based on temperature pathways from all IPCC scenarios combined with damage function specifications derived by Howard and Sterner (2025) through meta-analysis. Feeding scenario temperatures into level-effect damage functions yields an initial range of 0% to -7% of GDP driven purely by climate scenario uncertainty, while model uncertainty within a single scenario is captured separately; randomness has little effect on global damages. Introducing the full range of plausible damage functions widens the total estimate to between 1% and -37%, with the range expanding further into the future because these functions assume each additional degree of warming causes more damage than the previous one, confirming that damage function uncertainty is the dominant driver. The authors note some uncertainties can be reduced over time but argue reducing them will take time; waiting for excessive certainty risks delaying decisions. They recommend precautionary action and building resilience to plausible catastrophic outcomes rather than relying on models under deep uncertainty. Table A addresses which sources of uncertainty are reducible, though its contents are not detailed in the text. The authors clarify that these views are their own as Bank Underground contributors and do not necessarily reflect those of the Bank of England or its policy committees.
items.title: Sources of uncertainty in climate damage estimates

items.summary: EDF Energy, owned by the French state and Britain's fourth-largest supplier, plans to complete its takeover of pay-as-you-go specialist Utilita early next year. The deal would add 1.3m accounts to EDF's customer base, growing its share of the UK household energy market to more than 6m accounts, while bringing on board Utilita's 1,500 staff at an undisclosed price. Both companies will continue serving customers independently until the transaction concludes, and Utilita clients will be contacted about any service changes; EDF intends to keep operating from Utilita's headquarters near Southampton, home to roughly 600 of its employees. The acquisition follows a deal completed a year earlier in which EDF took on 47,000 standard credit accounts from Utilita as it sought to sharpen its focus on smart pay-as-you-go customers. Simone Rossi, chief executive of EDF's UK business, said the takeover would bring further expertise and represent a significant step toward growing EDF's UK customer base, while founder Bill Bullen said Utilita could continue offering best-in-class smart prepay solutions. The deal is likely to have strengthened Utilita financially after it briefly fell short of Ofgem's tougher financial resilience tests in an assessment in September 2025; Utilita confirmed being one of five suppliers that failed the rules last year but complied within months of the regulator flagging its position. For EDF, the acquisition supports a business where most large suppliers are losing customers: EDF lost about 280,000 accounts in the year after July 2025, while British Gas, Scottish Power and E.ON Next also shed customers, with Octopus Energy as the only major supplier to grow its market share. Utilita was founded in 2003 and became the first supplier to install a smart meter in 2008, modernising pay-as-you-go by enabling top-ups via app, website or phone instead of at corner shops or post offices. The transaction follows German group E.ON Next's purchase of struggling rival Ovo last month after competition watchdog approval, as households brace for sharp winter bill rises; consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast the quarterly price cap would jump 26% from January to around £2,166 a year for a typical household.
items.title: EDF acquires Utilita in UK energy market consolidation

items.summary: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Venezuela's new vice minister for AI and hydrocarbons, Albania del Mar Villarroel Gomez, said the country is deploying artificial intelligence to make its oil and gas industry more efficient and reduce emissions. She stated that Venezuelan policy is not to stop producing hydrocarbons but rather to cut waste while maintaining energy output. The government argues technology can reconcile continued fossil fuel production with efforts to limit environmental harm. Venezuela's upstream methane emissions intensity is nearly six times the global average, according to the International Energy Agency, and it remains the only major Central and South American energy producer that has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Villarroel said AI would be used to monitor emissions and methane leaks and improve oilfield operations. The approach places Venezuela on one side of a central dispute at COP31 over how the final agreement should address fossil fuel transition, with officials defending their right to exploit resources as part of economic recovery. US policy has pushed for higher Venezuelan output after capturing former leader Nicolas Maduro in January; Venezuela pumped about 1.2 million barrels per day in September and plans to reach 1.5 million bpd by the end of next year through state company PDVSA. Villarroel said she was named to her post earlier this year as vice minister for artificial intelligence and productive efficiency in hydrocarbons within the Ministry of Popular Power for Hydrocarbons. She noted Venezuela would favor smaller, specialized AI models over energy-intensive hyperscale systems because emissions monitoring and oilfield optimization require less computing power, with infrastructure powered primarily by its hydroelectric system, which she said supplies about 80 per cent of the country's electricity. When asked whether international technology companies were interested in working there, Villarroel declined to name them but acknowledged significant interest while emphasizing Venezuela would prioritize protecting national data and maintaining what it calls data sovereignty.
items.title: Venezuela Promotes AI to Clean Up Oil Production at COP31

items.summary: Binance stated that its plans to secure five additional operating licences in Asia remain on track despite a US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) cyberattack that struck the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange three weeks prior, with three of the licence applications already at an advanced stage. Binance's head of Asia-Pacific, SB Seker, told CNA during the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday (Nov 18) that the company has no intention to scale back its regional expansion and described regulator feedback as positive regarding how it managed the crisis. He noted that three licences are in very mature stages and imminent, though he did not identify the specific markets; Binance currently holds operating licences in more than 10 global markets, with South and Southeast Asia flagged as key priorities and further expansion details expected by the first quarter of 2027. Seker acknowledged a surge in withdrawals immediately after the attack but said activity had stabilised over recent days, with net inflows returning again; Binance has replenished part of its reserves used to cover losses and reported that day-to-day operations were not disrupted. The company attributed the incident to North Korean hackers who employed fake job interviews and malicious software, and since then has tightened internal controls, strengthened wallet-risk frameworks, and increased reliance on artificial intelligence tools to detect threats more quickly, while also working with partners in both crypto and AI sectors ahead of what it expects will be an ongoing wave of increasingly sophisticated attacks. Seker added that demand for digital assets remains strong across Asia, including Singapore, where he highlighted steepening engagement among retail users aged 18 to 36 as a market the company watches closely. Separately, Circle's chief commercial officer, Kash Razzaghi, said his firm was able to freeze about US$1.1 billion associated with the hack within days of the incident; the intervention underscored how stablecoin issuers can help contain fallout from major breaches and highlighted that many crypto thefts stem not from flaws in blockchain technology itself but from human error and social-engineering attacks, according to Razzaghi.
items.title: Binance Maintains Asia Expansion Plans After $6.3 Billion Hack

items.summary: Cambridge Sustainable Food has used leftover pumpkins to deliver its 1,000th free meal kit to low-income households. The organisation began producing recipe kits earlier this year from fruit and vegetables that would otherwise have gone to waste. After Halloween, it received large quantities of pumpkins from local farmers, including about 300kg (661lb) from a single supplier. Alex Vardill, who is 25 years old and part of the organisation, said many families receiving the kits sometimes struggle to access fresh produce, adding that this has helped improve food access at a time when food prices are high. The meal kits provide everything needed to make a meal in one bag with measurements already done and a recipe included. Vardill noted increased demand for both their services as it is described as a tough period for many people. The initiative launched in July using excess blackberries, with subsequent recipes themed around leftover tomatoes, courgettes, and apples. The Halloween leftovers were used to assemble 50 pumpkin and lentil soup recipe kits by volunteers this week. The kits are funded by Cambridge City Council and South Cambridgeshire District Council and distributed through food hubs and other local organisations. The organisation is based in a warehouse in the Barnwell area of Cambridge, which holds donated food from local supermarkets and residents.
items.title: Cambridge Sustainable Food Reaches 1,000th Free Meal with Pumpkin Recipe Kits

items.summary: After Jensen Huang, Nvidia's founder and former chief executive, resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs including an allegation involving a suspected Chinese spy, fashion commentators turned to his signature black Tom Ford leather jackets. Fashion journalist Emma Childs argued in The Cut that the garments had 'confessed before he did,' describing them as the outerwear of a man with an active Raya profile and a Harley-Davidson rather than one returning home to family after building the AI revolution. Michael Smith, co-host of the Pair of Kings podcast, added that Huang's jackets were stiff, unbroken in, and showed no creasing, which he read as evidence that 'if a man cannot commit to anything... what makes you think he can commit to you?' The jackets referenced are Tom Ford pieces so coveted that one sold at Sotheby's for nearly $1 million; the auction house called it not only a jacket but also 'the uniform of a first believer.' Huang has repeatedly said his wife and daughter buy the jackets, though Anand Giridharadas wrote in The New York Times that this claim rang hollow to fans who knew where each jacket came from, arguing Huang had 'betrayed the leather-jacket community' by cosplaying as a rebel while masking extraordinary power. Beyond infidelity readings, commentators offered other interpretations of the jackets' meaning. Behavioral psychologist Carolyn Mair told Salon that tech billionaires reject old-money sartorial codes to signal they need not conform because rules do not apply to them at their level; Stanford Law professor Richard Thompson Ford argued in an article by Vanessa Friedman that the jacket signals a down-to-earth rejection of fashionable artifice while still using fashion's power, evoking Marlon Brando and James Dean. Fashion director Vanessa Friedman noted executives like Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg understand that becoming popular culture rather than merely successful may depend on image, with Alvaro Fernandez-Espina calling it 'a modern armor' appropriating rebellion to certify victory over corporate scrutiny while giving a cool-villain aura fit for a spy movie. Derek Guy told Eugene Rabkin that leather in menswear telegraphs strength and rebellion, which middle-aged techno-oligarchs adopt to balance authority with youthful appeal amid tension between monetary capital and cultural cache. Critics including Thomas Frank lamented businessmen imagining themselves as rebels while becoming ideologists of business, stripping the garment of its original meaning. A viral image of Huang wearing a vintage studded Saint Laurent by Hedi Slimane jacket was later revealed in Vanity Fair to be AI-generated, completing an irony about the prophet of AI watching his signature garment reinvented by that technology. Following his resignation, President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that Tim Cook should replace him while saying he would not mind seeing Huang return; journalist Natasha Lee suggested a cardigan as a uniform 'nobody has ever been caught out by.'
items.title: Jensen Huang's leather jackets read as a confession of infidelity

items.summary: The International Energy Agency reported Thursday that carbon emissions linked to global data centers are projected to rise about 70% by 2030, as growing demand for artificial intelligence drives electricity consumption higher. In its annual World Energy Outlook 2026 report, the Paris-based agency projected that global electricity consumption by data centers would double to about 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI accounting for much of the increase. Data centers house the computer servers used to run AI systems and other digital services, requiring large amounts of electricity to operate and keep equipment cool. The expansion is expected to increase demand for electricity generated from fossil fuels, particularly in the United States and China, contributing to higher carbon emissions. The IEA projected that natural gas would supply about 60% of electricity used by US data centers by 2030, while coal would account for roughly half of the power consumed by China's AI data centers. In the European Union, renewable energy is expected to provide about 70% of data center electricity needs by the end of the decade. The agency also warned that rapid growth in electricity demand from AI infrastructure was putting additional pressure on power grids and equipment supply chains, highlighting the need for investment in electricity networks.
items.title: IEA projects 70% rise in data center carbon emissions by 2030

items.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA) reported Thursday that global demand for cooling buildings has overtaken demand for heating for the first time, attributing the shift to rising temperatures and higher household incomes. In its World Energy Outlook 2026, published in Istanbul on November 19, 2026, the agency noted that increasing incomes are making air conditioning more accessible, particularly in emerging and developing economies. The report highlighted a stark gap: outside China, 85% of households in these regions face high temperatures yet fewer than one in five owns an air conditioner. Under the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario, global electricity consumption for cooling is projected to rise by 1,700 terawatt-hours by 2035, a projection that already incorporates a gradual increase in average global temperatures. The agency warned that more intense, frequent and prolonged heat waves could push this figure significantly higher as households buy air conditioners and use them more often; under such conditions the projected increase could reach approximately 2,400 terawatt-hours by 2035, about 40% above the stated policies projection. This additional demand would strain electricity grids during peak periods when large numbers of households require cooling simultaneously. Air conditioning is one factor among several driving global electricity consumption, alongside industrial motors, electric vehicles, heat pumps and data centers. Since 2019, global electricity demand has grown by an average of 3.3% annually, more than double the 1.5% yearly growth in overall energy demand. Meeting this rising demand will require substantial investment in power infrastructure; the IEA estimated that at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines are needed worldwide over the next decade, and another 15 million kilometers of existing transmission and distribution lines must be upgraded or replaced.
items.title: Global Building Cooling Demand Overtakes Heating for First Time, IEA Reports

items.summary: As Anthropic prepares its initial public offering, seven co-founders who left OpenAI five years ago could each see their fortunes rise into the billions. The company plans to sell shares between $70 and $78 each, potentially valuing it at more than $1 trillion (€911.61 billion), placing it alongside Walmart and JPMorgan Chase and above Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors combined. If the IPO price reaches $78 (€71), each founder's shareholding could be worth at least $18.5bn (€16.86 billion). Dario Amodei, 43-year-old CEO who left OpenAI in 2020 citing concerns about commercial interests overriding AI safety, founded the company with his sister Daniela and five colleagues; she is now president after studying English literature at UC Santa Cruz and working for Matt Cartwright's office and Stripe. Tom Brown oversees computing resources following work on GPT-3 at Google DeepMind and OpenAI. Jared Kaplan directs scientific research while teaching physics scaling laws at Johns Hopkins University, having earned his Harvard PhD in physics. Chris Olah leads interpretability research after time at Google Brain and OpenAI, receiving a Thiel Fellowship before completing his degree at the University of Toronto. Jack Clark brings a journalism background from ZDNet UK, The Register and Bloomberg to lead public benefit work through the Anthropic Institute; he is the only founder born outside North America, having grown up in Brighton, UK. Sam McCandlish serves as chief architect on AI system design and risk policies after OpenAI safety work, holding PhDs from Stanford and undergraduate degrees from Brandeis University.
items.title: Anthropic founders' wealth set to surge with company's IPO

items.summary: Photographer-turned-entrepreneur Sha Hao relocated from Shanghai to Sydney to establish a virtual production studio, working alongside an Australian director who serves as his creative partner. The pair employ LED screens and virtual filming technology to produce short films for clients based in the United States. This arrangement is presented as demonstrating how China's hardware and software capabilities can be combined with Australia's creative talent to build a film production network spanning the Pacific Ocean.
items.title: Shanghai-to-Sydney Virtual Production Studio

items.summary:
Based on advance calculations by NASA, its Voyager 1 probe is believed to have reached a distance of one light-day from Earth approximately Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET (1016 GMT), marking a milestone no other spacecraft has achieved. The distance corresponds to about 26 billion kilometers, the span light travels in 24 hours. Because signals travel at the speed of light, JPL officials must wait roughly a day for confirmation from the probe and have scheduled an event on Thursday to discuss the achievement. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd called reaching one light-day "an astounding feat" she never expected to witness.

The spacecraft was launched in 1977 and is now the most distant human-made object, traveling at nearly 61,000 kilometers per hour. It crossed into interstellar space by passing through the heliosphere's outer edge in 2012; its twin, Voyager 2, also launched in 1977, entered interstellar space in 2018.

A JPL representative noted that recent power-saving measures may allow both Voyagers to remain in communication with Earth for three to four more years. The mission's goal is scientific research, and there is enough power to sustain the current instruments through next year's 50th launch anniversary; beyond that remains uncertain given the spacecraft are nearly 50 years old.

Voyager 1 continues gathering data after passing Jupiter and Saturn earlier in its journey. Its instruments have detected a faint hum from gas vibrations in interstellar space, while continuously transmitting measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma waves whenever the Deep Space Network points an antenna at it. Dodd reported that after crossing the heliopause, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the expected interstellar orientation but has instead retained its sun-governed direction; the team is watching for when rotation occurs. She also noted ongoing effects from solar activity, including coronal mass ejections whose shocks and pressure fronts reach Voyager 1 and beyond, prompting the question of where the sun's influence ends and pristine interstellar space begins.
items.title: NASA Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day Milestone

items.summary: Writing as an editor's note that his views do not necessarily reflect CGTN, Xin Ge of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics argues that global bay areas could provide the Asia-Pacific with practical platforms for cooperation amid rising protectionism. At the opening of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 on Wednesday morning at Shenzhen's Qianhai International Convention Center, President Xi Jinping called for establishing a global association for bay-area economic cooperation to strengthen exchanges among world-wide bay areas and explore deeper Asia-Pacific economic ties. Ge contends this initiative could complement APEC by translating regional consensus into concrete projects through closer links among ports, industrial parks, financial institutions and research centers, with examples including coordinated digital customs procedures and greener shipping, cross-border green investment, and joint research in artificial intelligence, biomedicine and advanced manufacturing. He emphasizes that the association's value depends on easing practical cross-border challenges such as customs procedures, product certification, payment arrangements and access to legal services rather than relying on summit declarations alone. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area is positioned as a natural anchor given its concentration of advanced manufacturing, universities, capital markets and international professional services across Shenzhen's innovation strengths, the Pearl River Delta's industrial base, Macao's cultural and tourism assets, and Hong Kong's links to global finance and business networks. Ge notes that for the region cooperation must move beyond physical connectivity toward harmonizing rules governing research funding, professional qualifications, commercial data and financial services while maintaining safeguards. He highlights Hong Kong's approaching 30th anniversary of its return on July 1, 2027 as an opportunity to leverage its complementary strengths in financing projects, structuring international transactions, resolving disputes and connecting mainland enterprises with overseas investors for green infrastructure, joint research and company expansion. Ge cautions that expectations should remain prudent since the association is still a proposal whose membership, mandate and working methods are undefined, it should complement rather than duplicate APEC or existing networks, and its benefits must extend beyond large corporations to smaller businesses, researchers and young entrepreneurs. He suggests a practical starting agenda of startup exchange programs, joint research funds, recognition of green-finance standards, digital trade facilitation and regular exchanges among port authorities and universities, with progress measured against public benchmarks rather than ambitious announcements. Ge concludes that the association's success will depend on making cross-border cooperation easier and more sustainable to turn regional commitments into tangible business outcomes as bay areas rely on open channels for trade, talent and investment.
items.title: China Proposes Global Bay-Area Economic Cooperation Association

items.summary: The People's Bank of China (PBOC) announced on Wednesday that it had signed the China-Canada Financial Working Group Terms of Reference with Canada's Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada. The signing clarifies the participating authorities, areas of cooperation, and communication methods for the working group, which is intended to operate regularly and institutionalized while strengthening communication between the two countries' financial regulators and deepening mutually beneficial sectoral cooperation. The group was established in January following a consensus reached by China's and Canada's leaders that year, with its first meeting held in Beijing in April. It will focus exchanges on developments in the financial sector, monetary policy, regulatory policies and practices, financial markets, financial stability, fintech, anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism, cross-border financial flows, and global financial governance. The two sides agreed to enhance collaboration by testing and discussing use of their recently renewed bilateral currency swap agreement, exploring expanded local-currency use in trade and investment, encouraging two-way investment, and promoting discussions on green and sustainable finance under multilateral platforms. They have already conducted technical exchanges on panda bond issuance, cross-border payment efficiency, anti-money laundering, and countering financing of terrorism. Both sides welcomed steps by the PBOC and Bank of Canada to implement their bilateral local currency swap arrangement; both welcomed eligible Canadian institutions issuing panda bonds in China, while Canada also welcomes and supports China's interest in issuing RMB-denominated green sovereign bonds in the Canadian market.
items.title: China-Canada Financial Working Group Signs Terms of Reference

items.summary:
Kemi Badenoch defended a remark she made to justify the Conservative plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. At Prime Minister's Questions, Labour leader Andy Burnham had demanded that she withdraw her “double amputees run marathons” comment, calling it crass and insensitive. On the Today programme this morning, Badenoch rejected the criticism, insisting she was delivering a message of hope rather than an attack on disabled people. She argued that if anyone can work then they should be encouraged to do so, using her example to suggest those with ADHD and mild anxiety should return to work. When presenter Nick Robinson challenged her by saying it is unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide for most disabled people, Badenoch disagreed, stating that governments routinely use extreme examples to illustrate points. She accused Robinson of faux outrage and tone policing, adding that while others are free to disagree, she knew where she stood.

The broadcast also covered several other stories. Tulip Siddiq said she was considering legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations from his administration that led to her resignation last year. On social media policy, Kemi Badenoch expressed concern about government intervention in getting a Russell Brand prison message video removed from YouTube, noting that while Brand had been convicted and is guilty under the law, his wife who posted the video was a separate person. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook confirmed the Ministry of Justice is in dialogue with Google over the removal but admitted they have no power to mandate it, since removal depends on the platform's own terms; Meta had already disabled Brand's Instagram and Facebook accounts after his conviction.

Badenoch also criticised a historic meeting between Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in China, describing it as disturbing because the three leaders appeared to be trying to carve up the world into a tri-polar arrangement with Russia taking Europe. She went further than Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who had been pressed by Ed Davey about the security implications of the meeting but stopped short of expressing concern.

The day's agenda included Louise Haigh answering questions in the Commons at 9.30am, James Cleverly expected to win more than 50% of the vote in the first round of Conservative voting for London mayor 2028, a Downing Street lobby briefing at 11.30am, Heather Hallett publishing her report on the test, trace and isolate system at noon, Chris Bryant attending a British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference meeting in Dublin, and Andy Burnham arriving in Berlin around 12.15pm for a pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing summit.
items.title: Badenoch Defends Amputee Comment on Disability Benefit Cuts

items.summary: The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, halting train services two days after a Ukrainian air raid destroyed the adjacent road bridge. Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, announced on Wednesday night that another attack had occurred and added Thursday that trains would resume crossing from approximately 4pm. Emergency repair crews reportedly made heroic efforts to restore the track, and Russia's transport ministry said nobody was wounded. The raid came hours before an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping. This marked the third time the $3.6bn bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, had been struck within a week; on Tuesday a 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed following a missile and drone attack planned over several weeks. Ukrainian military sources indicated the timing of the road bridge strike was deliberate ahead of the summit, suggesting the follow-up raid on the rail bridge may have been intended to bring it down as well. One source in Ukraine's armed forces said this week's attacks were designed to embarrass Putin globally, stating that destroying the bridge sends a message to Trump and Xi that Putin is not as strong as he pretends. For Ukraine, the bridge remains a hated symbol of Russian arrogance; Kyiv has declared it illegal and previously attempted twice to destroy it with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone the following year. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed his earlier attack on the road section as an unprecedented military operation that culminated a long campaign largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles, though he noted the railway line remained standing at that time. Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central road section bringing down its supporting arch, while Ukraine's Neptune cruise missile and the Ruta drone made by Dutch company Destinus targeted the adjacent rail section.
items.title: Kerch Rail Bridge Attacked Again Ahead of Trump-Putin-Xi Summit
